items.title: FASB proposes a fair value option for commodity inventories at financial institutions
items.summary: A proposed ASU published on 23 November would let certain financial institutions measure tangible commodity inventories at fair value. Comments are due by 7 January 2027.
detail: Today these institutions measure physical commodity inventories at the lower of cost and net realisable value, while the derivatives they use to manage the same positions are carried at fair value. The FASB says that creates an accounting mismatch.

Under the proposal, an entity would make an accounting policy election for each type of tangible commodity and would provide enhanced disclosures. The FASB says the election would better reflect how these institutions manage their commodity positions and would improve comparability.
items.why: It is a clear case study in measurement mismatch, a core theme when comparing US GAAP inventory rules with IAS 2 and its broker-trader fair value exception.

items.title: IFRS Interpretations Committee works through IFRS 18 questions
items.summary: The Committee met in London on 24 and 25 November to review comment letters on tentative agenda decisions, most of them about IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements. Outcomes have not yet been published.
detail: Agenda items included management-defined performance measures (hypothetical income and expenses, gross profit and public communications), a manufacturer-lessor's specified main business activities, operating expense presentation, subtotal labels, cash-related income and expenses, and classification for financing providers.
The agenda also covered an IFRS 10 question on control of a single-investor fund. Final agenda decisions are normally reported in the IFRIC Update that follows the meeting.
items.why: IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 from 2027, and these agenda decisions will shape how its new subtotals and performance measures are applied, including under the PSAK equivalent.

items.title: Wall Street rallies about 1.5% in a shortened Black Friday session
items.summary: US stocks rose in the half-day session on 27 November as AI and chip stocks rebounded, giving the S&P 500 a weekly gain of about 1.7%.
detail: Reports put the S&P 500 up between 1.5% and 1.6% at the 1 p.m. ET close, with the Nasdaq leading. The index had closed at 7,182.78 on 25 November, before the Thanksgiving holiday.

The S&P 500 is still down about 5% for November and would need to close above its 30 October level of 7,580.07 on Monday to finish the month higher. Treasury yields rose in the shortened session, with the 10-year near 4.91%, as traders keep pricing a Federal Reserve hike in December.
items.why: Rising yields alongside a stock rebound show how rate-hike expectations feed into discount rates and equity valuation.

items.title: WiseTech jumps 15% as the ASX 200 gains 2.8% for the week
items.summary: The ASX 200 rose 0.80% to 8,833.6 on Friday, led by technology stocks after a WiseTech trading update.
detail: The index added 69.8 points and the All Ordinaries rose 77.6 points to 8,943.7. Technology was the strongest sector with a gain of 3.63%, and gold miners also rose.
WiseTech shares climbed A$7.06 to A$53.87 after the company said revenue from its CargoWise platform grew 11% year on year in the four months to October. The ASX 200 gained 241 points over the week.
items.why: A single trading update moving a large-cap stock 15% is a reminder of how much weight markets put on interim disclosure.

items.title: Australian dollar climbs on a rebound in metal prices
items.summary: AUD/USD rose about 0.66% to around 0.6675 on Friday, outperforming other major currencies.
detail: FXStreet tied the move to a strong comeback in metal prices. The pair remained below its 20-day exponential moving average near 0.6758, which keeps the near-term technical bias negative.
The Australian dollar had touched an 11-month low near 0.656 earlier in the week, after weak October jobs data and October inflation of 4.9%.
items.why: For an Australian-based student with rupiah exposure, the AUD and IDR moves together set the effective cost of living and tuition.

items.title: Hong Kong gazettes updated global minimum tax rules
items.summary: Hong Kong said on 25 November it would gazette subsidiary legislation on 27 November to bring its global minimum tax rules into line with the latest OECD guidance. The rules take effect on 19 February 2027.
detail: The two instruments are the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Amendment of Schedules) Notice 2026 and the Tax Reserve Certificates (Fourth Series) (Amendment) Rules 2026. They amend the ordinance's schedules to take in OECD administrative guidance, consolidated commentary and safe harbours issued this year, and let officials prescribe certificate forms for global minimum tax and Hong Kong minimum top-up tax assessments.
The legislation goes to the Legislative Council on 2 December for negative vetting. Hong Kong's 15% minimum tax regime itself was passed in May 2025 and gazetted in June 2025.
items.why: It shows how jurisdictions keep importing OECD administrative guidance into domestic Pillar Two law; a useful comparison with Indonesia's PMK 136/2024.

items.title: OECD still building permanent de minimis and routine profit safe harbours
items.summary: EY's 25 November report says the Inclusive Framework is still developing a permanent Pillar Two safe harbour for multinationals' de minimis and routine profits.
detail: An OECD official said the aim is a permanent, stable safe harbour modelled on the transitional CbCR safe harbour, and that work on a Pillar Two risk assessment framework is ongoing.

The January 2026 side-by-side package had targeted the first half of 2026 for the permanent tests and extended the transitional CbCR safe harbour by one year to cover 2027. The transitional regime lets a jurisdiction qualify through a de minimis, simplified ETR or routine profits test.
items.why: Safe harbours decide how much GloBE computation groups must actually do, which is central to Pillar Two compliance cost.

items.title: Ravanelli wins High Court challenge over a £340,000 NIC bill
items.summary: The High Court ruled that HMRC wrongly refused to revisit a settlement over National Insurance on former footballer Fabrizio Ravanelli's Derby County earnings paid through an employee benefit trust.
detail: Part of Ravanelli's 2001 to 2003 Derby County pay went into an employee benefit trust. HMRC treated the trustee as the deemed employer and liable for NICs, and the trustee settled by paying about £1.2 million to HMRC, with the rest passed to Ravanelli.

Mr Justice Eardley found HMRC's refusal to reconsider was vitiated by a material error of law about who was liable. The court did not order repayment; HMRC must reassess the claim on the correct legal basis, and it says it is considering the judgment.
items.why: It is a useful judicial review example of how a public law error can reopen a tax settlement.

items.title: IHSG jumps 1.84% to 5,338 and gains 3.73% for the week
items.summary: The Jakarta Composite Index rose 96.30 points on Friday 27 November, its second strong session in a row.
detail: The index traded between 5,245.87 and 5,340.32 and closed at 5,338.46. Reports cited about Rp8.1 trillion in turnover and foreign net buying of around Rp769 billion.

Analysts linked the rally to optimism about efforts to restore the confidence of MSCI and foreign investors, including law enforcement by the authorities. Next week investors will watch the S&P Global manufacturing PMI, trade data and inflation.
items.why: The MSCI question is a live test of how governance and market structure feed into Indonesia's cost of capital.

items.title: Rupiah ends a losing streak at Rp18,330 as Asian currencies rise
items.summary: The rupiah strengthened 0.18% in the spot market on 27 November, a day after a record low close, but still lost 0.33% over the week.
detail: Bloomberg data cited by Kontan put the close at Rp18,330 per US dollar. Bank Indonesia's JISDOR reference rate was Rp18,375, from Rp18,390 the day before.
Traze Andalan Futures analyst Ibrahim Assuaibi expects the rupiah to stay vulnerable in a Rp18,330 to Rp18,400 range on Monday. The kurs pajak for 25 November to 1 December is Rp18,263.
items.why: JISDOR and kurs pajak are the rates used for translating foreign currency balances and tax amounts, so their drift matters for year-end reporting.

items.title: Government keeps the PTKP increase on the table for 2027
items.summary: Coordinating Minister Airlangga Hartarto says the plan to raise the non-taxable income threshold has not been cancelled, but no amount or start date has been set.
detail: Airlangga said on 13 November that the change would not start on 1 January. The Finance Ministry says it has received the proposal and is studying its effect on household purchasing power and on income tax revenue.
The current PTKP is Rp54 million a year, or Rp4.5 million a month. The idea discussed is to free workers on the regional minimum wage from income tax.
items.why: A PTKP change would directly alter PPh 21 withholding and the personal income tax base during a year of weak revenue.

items.title: OJK revokes BPR Bontang's licence after rescue fails
items.summary: OJK revoked the business licence of PT BPR Bontang in East Kalimantan on 25 November after capital recovery efforts failed, and LPS is liquidating the bank.
detail: The revocation is set out in OJK Board decision KEP-126/D.03/2026. LPS decided on 16 November to resolve the bank through liquidation and asked OJK to cancel its licence.
LPS will pay out guaranteed deposits and a liquidation team will settle the bank's rights and obligations. OJK asked customers to stay calm because deposits are covered by the LPS guarantee.
items.why: It illustrates Indonesia's bank resolution chain from OJK supervision to LPS liquidation.

worth.title: Hong Kong gazettes updated global minimum tax rules
worth.text: A neat example of how OECD administrative guidance flows into domestic Pillar Two law, useful when comparing with Indonesia's PMK 136/2024.
